title: Clear Academic and Professional Writing

sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Think of a thesis like the destination typed into a GPS. The hook is the person waving you into the car, and the conclusion is saying "we made it." But the destination is the one line that decides every turn you take along the way. If you never type a destination, you just drive around, and that is exactly what a paper without a real thesis feels like to a reader.

### Question 2

Think about a weather forecast. If the radar shows a few clouds, the forecaster says "it may rain later." If a huge storm is twenty minutes away, they say "it will rain." Both are being honest, because each one matched their words to how much the radar actually showed. Announcing "it will definitely rain" after seeing two clouds is not brave, it is just wrong, and people stop trusting that forecaster. Words like "may" and "suggests" are a writer's way of telling you how much radar they are looking at.

### Question 3

Concise writing is like packing a backpack for a hike. You bring the water and the map, and you leave out the third pair of shoes. Concise does not mean short for the sake of short. It means nothing in the bag that is not pulling its weight, so the important stuff is easy to grab.

### Question 4

Imagine texting a friend who is walking home: "there's some pizza left." Some could mean one slice or most of the box, so your friend still has to guess. "Three slices are left and the garlic bread is gone" tells them exactly what they will find in the kitchen. Words like decent, good, and adequate are guessing words, while numbers and named things are seeing words. In a chart, the next person makes real decisions from your sentence, so give them something they can actually picture.

### Question 5

Imagine a name tag floating in the air with nobody wearing it. Your eyes stick it on whoever is standing closest, which might be the wrong person entirely. "Running down the hall, the chart fell" makes it sound like the chart was jogging. Fix it by making sure the person the phrase describes is the very next thing you name.

### Question 6

Picture stepping stones across a creek. Even if every stone is solid, if they sit too far apart you cannot cross. Phrases like "however," "as a result," and "this pattern" are stones placed close enough to step on. Strong evidence is the rock itself; coherence is the spacing that lets a reader actually walk across it.

### Question 7

A list is like a row of matching chairs. If two are dining chairs and one is a beanbag, your eye trips over the odd one out. "Writing, citing, revising" all wear the same -ing uniform, so the row looks even. Dropping "to cite" into that row is the beanbag.

### Question 8

Some phrases are packing peanuts: they fill the box but they are not the gift. "Due to the fact that" is a five-word way of saying "because." "Are considered to be incomplete" is a long way to say "are incomplete." Pull out the peanuts and the same idea arrives in half the space.

### Question 9

There are three ways to say something: too casual, too puffed up, and just right. "Totally freaking out" is a text to your friend. "Affective dysregulation during evaluative performance episodes" is showing off. "I felt anxious, and my hands were less steady" is a real person telling you exactly what happened. Big words are not the same thing as professional words.

### Question 10

You would not paint the walls of a house before deciding where the rooms go. If a whole wall gets knocked down tomorrow, that paint job was wasted. Revising means moving walls; editing means painting. Do the big structural moves first, then make the surfaces look sharp.

### Question 11

Imagine tracing someone else's drawing and swapping the crayon colors. You changed the colors, but the lines are still theirs. A real paraphrase means closing the book, saying the idea out loud in your own way, then writing that down and naming who you got it from. Both halves matter: your sentence shape and their name.

### Question 12

The verb is a sentence's engine. Turning "decided" into "the making of a decision" takes the engine out and leaves "occurred" to push the car instead. The sentence still gets somewhere, but slowly, and the driver is now sitting in the back seat. Keep the doer up front and let a real verb do the work.
